slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure portal, create a Storage Account with ADLS Gen2 enabled (hierarchical namespace on), then create two containers -- name one something a governed organization would recognize, like "raw-customer-data" -- and build a few nested directories inside it.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or Azure CLI output showing one Storage Account with ADLS Gen2 enabled, two containers, and at least 3 nested directories inside one container.

slots.practicalActivity: On the storage account from the previous hour, assign an RBAC role (e.g., Storage Blob Data Contributor) to your own account at the container level, then write down, as if for a data access policy, which ACL read/write/execute permissions you'd set on one directory and which Azure resource would use a managed identity to read it without stored credentials.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot confirming the RBAC role assignment, plus a one-paragraph access policy naming the ACL permissions for one directory and the managed-identity scenario.

lessons.title: CSV vs. JSON vs. Parquet vs. Delta

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a SAS token for one container (read-only, short expiry) and test downloading a file with it; then save the same small sample dataset as CSV, JSON, and (if possible) Parquet, compare file sizes, and write a date-based partitioning folder scheme for that dataset.
slots.deliverable: A working SAS URL that successfully downloads a blob, plus a short written partitioning plan (folder structure) for the sample dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a full data lake folder structure in your storage account implementing raw/cleansed/curated zones, and within curated, lay out bronze/silver/gold directories, uploading one small sample file into each zone to prove the structure works.
slots.deliverable: A storage account screenshot showing the raw/cleansed/curated and bronze/silver/gold folder structure, each containing at least one sample file.

slots.practicalActivity: Hands-on lab: starting from an empty storage account, recreate the entire Chapter 1 data lake design end to end -- containers, hierarchical namespace, an RBAC role assignment, a SAS token for one zone, and the raw/cleansed/curated plus bronze/silver/gold folder layout -- without referring back to the lesson videos.
slots.deliverable: A fully built storage account matching the chapter's described architecture, captured in a short screenshot walkthrough or Azure CLI script that recreates it.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page design document proposing a data lake architecture for a hypothetical company's customer data: the zone structure, which zone uses RBAC vs. SAS tokens for access, the file format chosen for each zone and why, and the partitioning strategy for the curated zone -- noting which zone would need the strictest access control if this data were later classified as sensitive.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written data lake design document covering zones, access control choice, file formats, and partitioning strategy.

slots.practicalActivity: In a Python file or notebook, declare a variable of each core type (int, float, str, bool, list, dict) representing a sample customer record (customer_id, email, is_active, etc.), then print each one's type with type().
slots.deliverable: A .py or notebook file with one variable of each core data type representing a sample customer record, each printed with its type.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a Python list of 5 dictionaries representing sample customer records (fields like email, phone, signup_date), then write conditional logic that flags a record as "incomplete" if email or phone is missing and "complete" otherwise.
slots.deliverable: A script with a list of 5 customer dictionaries and conditional logic correctly labeling at least one record as incomplete and others as complete.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a function that loops over the list of customer dictionaries from the previous slot to count how many records are complete vs. incomplete, returning both counts.
slots.deliverable: A working Python function, called on your sample customer list, that prints the complete and incomplete record counts.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a function that reads a small CSV file of customer records from disk, wrapped in try/except to handle a missing file or malformed row gracefully, printing a clear error message instead of crashing.
slots.deliverable: A script that successfully reads a valid CSV, and when pointed at a missing or bad file instead prints a handled error message rather than crashing.

slots.practicalActivity: Load a small sample CSV and a small sample JSON file of customer-style data into two separate pandas DataFrames, then inspect each with .head(), .info(), and .describe() -- noting any columns with unexpected null counts as you go.
slots.deliverable: A notebook or script showing two DataFrames (from CSV and JSON) with .head(), .info(), and .describe() output for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Use Python's requests library to call a free public REST API, parse the JSON response, and load the relevant fields into a pandas DataFrame; then flatten any nested structure in that response into a clean tabular form with pandas' json_normalize.
slots.deliverable: A script that calls a real public API and loads at least 3 relevant fields into a pandas DataFrame, plus the json_normalize code that flattens any nested JSON in the response.

slots.practicalActivity: Use pyodbc or sqlalchemy to connect to a local SQL Server instance and write the previous slot's DataFrame into a staging table; then, on a deliberately messy sample CSV (duplicate rows, nulls, inconsistent casing/whitespace), write a cleaning function using pandas that dedupes rows, fills or drops nulls, and standardizes text columns.
slots.deliverable: A staging table in a local SQL Server database populated by a Python script, plus a before/after row count proving the cleaning function removed duplicates, handled nulls, and standardized at least one text column.

lessons.title: Building a Simple Python ETL Process

slots.practicalActivity: Combine everything from this chapter into one script: extract customer data from a CSV (or the REST API from an earlier slot), transform it with the cleaning logic from the previous slot, and load the result into a SQL Server staging table.
slots.deliverable: One end-to-end Python ETL script (extract, transform, load) that populates a real SQL Server table from source data.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Python for Data Engineers: build a standalone Python ETL tool that reads a raw sample CSV, cleans and enriches it, and writes both a cleaned CSV and a SQL Server table as two separate load targets -- all driven from one script with proper exception handling throughout, and a short code comment at each stage noting what a data quality check on that stage would look for.
slots.deliverable: A single Python script producing both a cleaned CSV file and a populated SQL Server table from one raw input file, with try/except handling around each I/O step and a data-quality comment at each stage.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short comparison of running a large aggregation on a single machine with pandas vs. a distributed Spark cluster, then sign in to a Spark environment (Databricks Community Edition or a local PySpark install) to confirm it's running.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison (single machine vs. distributed) plus confirmation (screenshot or output) that a Spark session is running in your environment.

slots.practicalActivity: In your Spark environment's UI, identify the driver and at least one executor for a running or sample job, and sketch the architecture (driver, cluster manager, executors) as applied to that specific job.
slots.deliverable: A labeled diagram or screenshot identifying the driver and executors for one real Spark job in your environment.

slots.practicalActivity: Load a sample dataset into a Spark DataFrame and check its number of partitions with .rdd.getNumPartitions(), then repartition it to a different number and confirm the partition count changed.
slots.deliverable: Output showing the original partition count and the changed partition count after repartitioning the same DataFrame.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a chain of Spark transformations (filter, select) on a sample DataFrame and confirm nothing executes until you call an action like .count() or .show(); use .explain() before and after the action to observe lazy evaluation in the query plan.
slots.deliverable: Captured .explain() output showing the unexecuted logical plan, plus the result after triggering it with an action.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a SparkSession explicitly in code, use it to read a sample CSV or Parquet file into a Spark DataFrame, and print its schema with .printSchema().
slots.deliverable: A script that explicitly creates a SparkSession, loads a file into a DataFrame, and prints its schema.

slots.practicalActivity: Register the DataFrame from the previous slot as a temporary SQL view and run a Spark SQL query against it using spark.sql(), comparing the result to the equivalent DataFrame API call.
slots.deliverable: A Spark SQL query and its DataFrame-API equivalent, both producing the same result against the same temp view.

slots.practicalActivity: Hands-on lab: start a fresh Spark session, load a sample dataset, inspect its partitioning, run a chain of lazy transformations followed by one action, and finish by querying it with Spark SQL from a registered temp view -- documenting each architecture concept (driver/executor, partitions, lazy evaluation) as you go.
slots.deliverable: A single notebook or script walking through SparkSession creation, partition inspection, lazy transformations plus an action, and a Spark SQL query, with a one-line note under each step naming the concept it demonstrates.

slots.practicalActivity: Using PySpark, create a DataFrame manually from a small Python list of tuples, then read a real sample CSV file into a second DataFrame with spark.read.csv(), comparing their schemas.
slots.deliverable: A script showing a manually created DataFrame and a CSV-loaded DataFrame, with both schemas printed.

slots.practicalActivity: Read the same sample dataset in JSON and Parquet formats (converting a sample with df.write if only CSV is available), and compare load times and the inferred schemas across all three formats.
slots.deliverable: Three DataFrames (CSV, JSON, Parquet) loaded from the same underlying data, with a short note comparing load time and schema accuracy.

slots.practicalActivity: Define an explicit StructType schema for your sample DataFrame (correct types for IDs, dates, and amount fields) and reload the data using it instead of schema inference, then use .select() to pull only a few key columns into a new DataFrame.
slots.deliverable: A DataFrame loaded with an explicit schema (not inferred), plus a .select() result containing only the named columns.

slots.practicalActivity: Use .filter()/.where() to remove rows failing an obvious validity rule (a negative amount or an empty required field), then use .withColumn() to add a computed column (e.g., a derived date or category field).
slots.deliverable: A filtered DataFrame (invalid rows removed) with a new computed column added via withColumn().

slots.practicalActivity: Use when()/otherwise() to bucket records into a new tier column based on a numeric field's ranges, then use type conversion functions to ensure that numeric field and any date fields are proper, non-string types.
slots.deliverable: A DataFrame with a tier column correctly bucketing records, and confirmed numeric/date (not string) types on the relevant columns.

slots.practicalActivity: Use string functions to clean up a text column (trimming/upper-casing a name or category field) and use date functions (year(), month(), dayofweek()) to extract year, month, and day-of-week into new columns.
slots.deliverable: A DataFrame with one cleaned text column and three new date-derived columns (year, month, day of week).

slots.practicalActivity: Check your DataFrame for nulls column by column, drop or fill rows with critical nulls, then identify and remove exact duplicate rows with dropDuplicates() -- the same two data quality problems a downstream governance check would flag.
slots.deliverable: A before/after row count showing nulls handled and duplicate rows removed from the dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Use .groupBy() on a category or date column with .agg() to compute record count, average of a numeric field, and total of that field per group.
slots.deliverable: A grouped/aggregated DataFrame showing record count, average, and total per group.

slots.practicalActivity: Join your main DataFrame to a small lookup DataFrame (an ID-to-name mapping), then use union() to combine two separately-filtered subsets of records back into one DataFrame.
slots.deliverable: A joined DataFrame showing real lookup values on the main rows, plus a union() result recombining two filtered subsets.

slots.practicalActivity: Use a window function (Window.partitionBy + orderBy) to compute a running total within each group over time, then register the result as a temporary view with createOrReplaceTempView().
slots.deliverable: A window-function result showing a running total per group over time, registered as a usable temp view.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite one of the previous slot's Spark SQL queries using the DataFrame API instead, confirming identical results, then write the final cleaned/aggregated DataFrame out to disk with .write.parquet().
slots.deliverable: A DataFrame-API query matching a prior Spark SQL result, plus a Parquet file written to disk from the final DataFrame.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite the Parquet write from the previous slot to partition the output by a date column (partitionBy("load_date")), then inspect the resulting folder structure and apply one performance fundamental (caching a DataFrame you reuse, or reducing partition count before a final write) to the full pipeline.
slots.deliverable: A partitioned Parquet output (one subfolder per date value) plus a documented performance change (caching or repartitioning) applied to the pipeline.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone-style lab for PySpark: build one end-to-end script that reads raw sample data, applies your Chapter 4 cleaning pipeline, computes group-level aggregations with groupBy and window functions, joins in lookup values, and writes the final result out as date-partitioned Parquet -- running the whole thing from a single script, start to finish.
slots.deliverable: One complete PySpark script that goes from raw CSV/JSON input to a final, date-partitioned Parquet output, incorporating cleaning, joins, and aggregation.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page technical summary of the full pipeline you built in the previous lab: what each stage does, which PySpark operations were used at each step, and one specific change you'd make to add data quality checkpoints (null rates, duplicate rates, referential checks against the lookup table) before this pipeline feeds a governed, production dataset.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written pipeline summary covering each stage, the operations used, and one concrete data-quality checkpoint you'd add before production use.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can provision and secure an Azure data lake with a real zone structure, write Python scripts that extract, clean, and load real data, and build and tune working PySpark pipelines -- the storage, scripting, and compute foundation the rest of the Data Governance Engineer path assumes when it teaches policies, quality rules, and stewardship over that same data.
